sections.normalized_html:
We are given a right triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] with legs of length [MATH: AB = 5] and [MATH: BC = 12,] and an altitude [MATH: \overline{BD}] dropped from [MATH: B] to hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}.]

First, we calculate the length of the hypotenuse [MATH: \overline{AC}.] According to the Pythagorean Theorem, [MATH: AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2.] Therefore, we have [MATH: AC|= sqrt(AB^{2} + BC^{2}); = sqrt(5^{2} + 12^{2}); = sqrt(25 + 144); = sqrt(169); = 13.]

Next, consider the triangles [MATH: \triangle ADB] and [MATH: \triangle ABC.] Both triangles share [MATH: \angle A,] and both contain a right angle: [MATH: \angle ADB] and [MATH: \angle ABC,] respectively.

So, by the AA similarity criterion, the triangles are similar.

Since [MATH: \triangle ADB \sim \triangle ABC,] the ratios of corresponding sides are equal. In particular, [MATH: \dfrac{DB}{BC} = \dfrac{AB}{AC}.]

Substituting in the known values, we have [MATH: \dfrac{BD}{12} = \dfrac{5}{13}.]

Finally, solving for [MATH: BD,] we get [MATH: BD|= (5)/(13) ⋅ 12; = (60)/(13); ≈ 4.62.]

Therefore, the length of [MATH: \overline{BD}] is [MATH: 4.62.]

sections.normalized_html:
In the figure above, [MATH: TX=8] and [MATH: RX=15.] What is the length of [MATH: \overline{XY}]?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/ef4d724078082de7c5338f0bfe9f188c]

In the figure above, [MATH: TX=8] and [MATH: RX=15.] What is the length of [MATH: \overline{XY}]?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

sections.normalized_html:
Applying the Pythagorean Theorem to [MATH: \triangle{RXT},] we can obtain [MATH: RT] as follows: [MATH: RT^{2}|= TX^{2} + RX^{2}; RT^{2}|= 8^{2} + 15^{2}; RT^{2}|= 64 + 225; RT^{2}|= 289; RT|= 17]

From the diagram, we can see that [MATH: \triangle{RYT}] and [MATH: \triangle{RXT}] are right triangles that have the non-right angle [MATH: \angle{R}] as a common angle. Therefore, [MATH: \triangle{RYT} \sim \triangle{RXT}] by the AA Similarity Criterion. As a consequence of the similarity, we obtain [MATH: \dfrac{RY}{RT} = \dfrac{RT}{RX}.]

Substituting the values for [MATH: RT] and [MATH: RX] into the equality above, and solving for [MATH: RY,] we obtain [MATH: (RY)/(17)|= (17)/(15); (RY)/(17)|= (17)/(15); RY|= 17 ⋅ (17)/(15); RY|= (289)/(15).]

Finally, note that [MATH: XY = RY - RX.]

Therefore, [MATH: XY|= (289)/(15) − 15; = (289)/(15) − (225)/(15); = (289 − 225)/(15); = (64)/(15).]

So, the length of [MATH: \overline{XY}] is [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{64}{15}}.]

items.title: Determining Possible Values of a Side Length in Embedded Right Triangles

sections.normalized_html:
In the figure above, [MATH: \triangle{XYZ}] has an area between [MATH: 70] and [MATH: 90,] inclusive, and [MATH: q] is an integer. What is the largest possible value of [MATH: p?]

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/b2b98422ee75d654497164d3aa737338]

In the figure above, [MATH: \triangle{XYZ}] has an area between [MATH: 70] and [MATH: 90,] inclusive, and [MATH: q] is an integer. What is the largest possible value of [MATH: p?]

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.

sections.normalized_html:
The formula for the area of a triangle is [MATH: \mathcal{A} = \dfrac{b \cdot h}{2},] where [MATH: b] is a base and [MATH: h] is the corresponding height.

In the case of [MATH: \triangle{XYZ},] from the diagram we can see that its base is [MATH: b = 3 + 17 = 20,] and its corresponding height is [MATH: h = q.]

Therefore, the area of [MATH: \triangle{XYZ}] is [MATH: A|= (b ⋅ h)/(2); = (20 ⋅ q)/(2); = 10q.]

We are told that the area is between [MATH: 70] and [MATH: 90,] inclusive. Thus, we have the following compound inequality: [MATH: 70 \leq 10q \leq 90.]

Dividing by [MATH: 10] to isolate [MATH: q,] we obtain [MATH: 7 \leq q \leq 9.] Since [MATH: q] is an integer, its possible values are [MATH: 7,] [MATH: 8,] and [MATH: 9.]

Looking at the diagram again, we can see that the two right triangles are similar: each has a right angle, and they share the angle [MATH: \angle{X}.] As a consequence of this similarity, we obtain [MATH: \dfrac{p}{q} = \dfrac{3}{3 + 17}.]

Solving for [MATH: p,] we get [MATH: (p)/(q)|= (3)/(3 + 17); (p)/(q)|= (3)/(20); p|= (3q)/(20).]

Now, from the possible values of [MATH: q,] we will find the possible values of [MATH: p.]

  • For [MATH: q = 7,] we obtain [MATH: p = \dfrac{3(7)}{20} = \dfrac{21}{20}.]

  • For [MATH: q = 8,] we obtain [MATH: p = \dfrac{3(8)}{20} = \dfrac{24}{20} = \dfrac{6}{5}.]

  • For [MATH: q = 9,] we obtain [MATH: p = \dfrac{3(9)}{20} = \dfrac{27}{20}.]

Therefore, the largest possible value of [MATH: p] is [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{27}{20}}.]
